title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Ten Years of Chemistry, Cash Conversion, and Capital Compression

epigraph.quote: Accrual earnings can flatter a single quarter, but ten years of operating cash flow and balance-sheet capital employed never lie.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Maxim

web_blocks.html: A twelve-year review from FY15 through FY26 (plus H1 FY27) shows why Aurobindo is a capital-cycle transition story [1]. Consolidated sales nearly tripled from ₹12,103 crore in FY15 to ₹33,653 crore in FY26, hitting ₹36,913 crore TTM in September 2026 [1]. Even so, growth was uneven. Five-year sales CAGR through FY26 slowed to 6.32% as US generic deflation offset Europe [1]. Growth then snapped back to +16% YoY in Q1 FY27 and +24% YoY in Q2 FY27 [1][3].

web_blocks.caption: 12-Year Consolidated Profit & Loss Statement (Mar 2015–Mar 2026 & TTM Sep 2026, INR Crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating margins compressed from 23% (FY16–18) to a 15% trough in FY23 before stabilizing at 20–21% (FY24–TTM Sep 2026); note FY21 PAT (₹5,334 Cr) was boosted by ₹3,195 Cr of one-off Other Income [1].

web_blocks.html: Two accounting items stand out in the Profit & Loss statement. First, FY21 Net Profit of ₹5,334 crore included ₹3,195 crore of one-off Other Income from the Natrol sale [1]. Excluding that gain, core operating profit plateaued from FY20 to FY23 before rising to ₹5,826 crore in FY24, ₹6,560 crore in FY25, and ₹6,870 crore in FY26 [1]. Second, Depreciation more than tripled from ₹558 crore in FY18 to ₹1,778 crore in FY26 [1]. It reached ₹531 crore in Q2 FY27 (~₹2,124 crore annualized) as new plants went live [1].

web_blocks.caption: 12-Year Consolidated Cash Flow Statement (Mar 2015–Mar 2026, INR Crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Cumulative 10-year CFO (FY17–FY26) totaled ₹33,884 Cr against ₹29,997 Cr of cumulative PAT (113% cash conversion), with FY26 CFO hitting ₹5,526 Cr and FCF rebounding to ₹2,468 Cr [1].

web_blocks.html: Cash conversion is a clear bright spot. From FY17 through FY26, Aurobindo generated ₹33,884 crore in Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) against ₹29,997 crore in Net Profit [1]. That equals a 113% CFO-to-PAT conversion ratio [1]. In FY26 alone, CFO hit ₹5,526 crore (158% of PAT), funding ₹3,058 crore of capex and leaving ₹2,468 crore in Free Cash Flow [1]. Still, cash flow has been cyclical. Heavy capex in FY23 (-₹3,971 Cr) and FY24 (-₹4,242 Cr) led to negative FCF (-₹323 Cr and -₹1,067 Cr) during peak Pen-G and biologics construction [1].

web_blocks.caption: 12-Year Consolidated Balance Sheet (Mar 2015–Sep 2026, INR Crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Gross Fixed Assets + CWIP expanded 6x from ₹4,126 Cr (Mar 2015) to ₹24,902 Cr (Sep 2026), with CWIP dropping from ₹5,214 Cr (Mar 2026) to ₹3,487 Cr (Sep 2026) as major projects capitalized [1].

web_blocks.caption: 12-Year Working Capital & Return Ratios (Mar 2015–Mar 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: ROCE compressed from 27% (FY15–16) to 13% (FY26) due to ₹18,000+ Cr of capital expansion and 326-day inventory, even as stretched payables (151 days) kept net working capital at 44 days [1].

web_blocks.title: Forensic Flags: Capitalized Interest, 326-Day Inventory & ROCE Compression
paragraphs: 1. Capitalized Interest & Rising Depreciation: CWIP peaked at ₹5,214 Cr in March 2026 alongside ₹8,073 Cr in gross debt (₹8,630 Cr by Sep 2026) [1]. Management capitalized interest on greenfield builds, keeping FY26 P&L interest at ₹384 Cr [1]. In H1 FY27, CWIP fell by ₹1,727 Cr as Fixed Assets rose by ₹4,008 Cr [1]. As a result, Q2 FY27 depreciation jumped to ₹531 Cr, and P&L interest will rise [1].

2. ROCE & ROE Compression: ROCE dropped from 27% (FY15–16) to 9% (FY23) and 13% (FY26), while 3-year ROE sits at 10.8% (10.1% latest) [1]. Lifting ROCE above 16–18% requires scaling Pen-G, China, CuraTeQ, and TheraNym without another 326-day inventory buildup [1].

3. Balance-Sheet Cushion: Gross debt stood at ₹8,630 Cr (Sep 2026) against ₹39,400 Cr in net worth (0.22x debt-to-equity) [1]. Aurobindo ended FY26 with ₹10,676 Cr in cash and ₹3,002 Cr in net cash [1][2]. That buffer easily covers remediation and Unit 2 CDMO capex [17].

web_blocks.html: Asset-Turn Inflection Watch: Gross Fixed Assets plus CWIP grew sixfold from ₹4,126 crore in FY15 to ₹24,902 crore in September 2026 [1]. Between March and September 2026, CWIP fell by ₹1,727 crore as active fixed assets rose by ₹4,008 crore [1]. That shift proves major greenfield plants are now in commercial service. If Pen-G, Europe, and CuraTeQ scale without fresh working-capital bloat, asset turns will lift ROCE back toward 16%–18% [1][11][16].

book_paragraphs: Now let's open the ten-year forensic ledger—because in capital-intensive manufacturing, the income statement only tells half the story. Between FY15 and FY26, Aurobindo grew sales from ₹12,103 crore to ₹33,653 crore, and TTM sales through September 2026 reached ₹36,913 crore. Yet over the five years ending FY26, annual revenue growth averaged just 6.32%, and operating margins swung from 23% down to 15% in FY23 before recovering to 20%–21%. Also note a classic accounting trap in FY21: reported profit of ₹5,334 crore included ₹3,195 crore of one-off other income, not core drug earnings.

Where Aurobindo passes a crucial forensic test is cash conversion. Over the ten years from FY17 through FY26, cumulative operating cash flow totaled ₹33,884 crore against ₹29,997 crore of net profit—113% conversion. In FY26 alone, ₹5,526 crore of operating cash flow covered ₹3,058 crore of capex and still left ₹2,468 crore in free cash flow. That is why, even after spending heavily on Kakinada, China, and Hyderabad biologics, Aurobindo ended FY26 with ₹3,002 crore in net cash.

The price of that buildout shows up on the balance sheet. Fixed assets plus capital work-in-progress swelled sixfold from ₹4,126 crore in FY15 to ₹24,902 crore by September 2026. Notice that between March and September 2026, work-in-progress dropped by ₹1,727 crore while active fixed assets jumped by ₹4,008 crore—proof that multi-year projects are finally going live. At the same time, capitalizing interest during construction kept FY26 P&L interest artificially low at ₹384 crore, and heavy asset additions compressed ROCE from 27% a decade ago to 13% today, with ROE around 10.1%.

Putting all six chapters together, Aurobindo is not a frictionless asset-light compounder. It is a heavily capitalized industrial pharma platform at the tail end of a massive investment cycle, backed by a net-cash balance sheet and 113% ten-year cash conversion—but carrying real execution risk on inventory turns (326 days) and Eugia's USFDA remediation.

Let's double-check two subtle accounting items in those ten-year tables so nothing catches us off guard later. First, look at the 'capitalizing interest cost' flag raised in fundamental screens. Between FY21 and FY26, Aurobindo carried ₹3,062 crore to ₹5,214 crore in Capital Work-in-Progress while holding ₹5,286 crore to ₹8,630 crore in gross borrowings. Under accounting rules, interest on debt funding active greenfield construction is capitalized onto the balance sheet rather than expensed on the P&L. That is why FY26 P&L interest was only ₹384 crore even on ₹8,073 crore of year-end debt. Now that CWIP fell by ₹1,727 crore between March and September 2026 as projects went live, you should expect higher depreciation (already ₹531 crore in Q2 FY27) and a slightly higher P&L interest run-rate.

Second, look at the trajectory of return on capital employed. A decade ago, in FY15 and FY16, Aurobindo earned 27% ROCE on a ₹4,126 crore fixed-asset base. By FY26, fixed assets plus CWIP had grown to ₹22,621 crore (and ₹24,902 crore by September 2026), compressing ROCE to 13% and ROE to 10.1%. That compression is not a sign of a broken business—operating cash flow hit a record ₹5,526 crore in FY26—but it is a clear reminder that Aurobindo has already paid the upfront capital bill. Now, over the next three years, revenue and operating profit must grow into that ₹25,000 crore asset base.

Before we leave the price-blind fundamentals and step into valuation, let's pause on one more forensic check in the ten-year cash flow statement: how Aurobindo funded its ₹17,000+ crore capex and investment wave without blowing up its balance sheet. Between FY17 and FY26, cumulative operating cash flow of ₹33,884 crore exceeded cumulative net profit of ₹29,997 crore by ₹3,887 crore—a 113% conversion rate that almost no mid-tier generic peer matches. Even in FY26, when depreciation climbed to ₹1,778 crore and capex absorbed ₹3,058 crore, Free Cash Flow snapped back to ₹2,468 crore.

That cash-generation resilience explains why Aurobindo carries ₹10,676 crore in cash and liquid investments against ₹7,673 crore of gross debt at FY26-end (₹8,630 crore gross borrowings by September 2026), leaving roughly ₹3,002 crore in net cash. In plain English, Aurobindo is not financially fragile. It can fund TheraNym's $175 million Unit 2 mammalian bioreactor expansion and absorb Eugia remediation consulting costs out of internal accruals without diluting shareholders or begging banks for covenant waivers.

Yet financial solvency is not the same thing as capital efficiency. With ₹24,902 crore now sitting in gross fixed assets and CWIP as of September 2026—six times the ₹4,126 crore base in FY15—Aurobindo must prove over FY27–FY29 that asset turns can lift ROCE from 13% back toward 16%–18%. Until sterile FDA clearances and working-capital normalization arrive, this remains a conditional cyclical recovery rather than an effortless compounder.

One helpful way to stress-test Aurobindo's balance sheet is to ask what happens if the next two years turn rocky. Suppose US generic pricing softens or sterile remediation takes longer than management hopes. Even in that slower scenario, Aurobindo enters FY27 with ₹10,676 crore in cash and liquid investments against ₹7,673 crore of FY26-end gross debt (₹8,630 crore gross borrowings by September 2026), leaving ₹3,002 crore of net cash and a modest 0.22x gross debt-to-equity ratio.

That means Aurobindo is highly unlikely to face a liquidity crunch or forced equity dilution. The real risk is not solvency—it is opportunity cost: if newly capitalized plants take longer to reach full utilization, consolidated ROCE could linger in the low teens rather than climbing back toward 16%–18%.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Ten years of 113% CFO-to-PAT conversion and a ₹3,002 crore net-cash cushion prove that Aurobindo's core cash engine is real. The entire underwriting debate now hinges on asset turn: can the ₹24,902 crore fixed-asset base lift ROCE back above 16% as Pen-G, Europe, and biologics scale?
